public_rationale: "Generative AI is not automation" describes what kind of thing the technology is. He gives no definition, measure or period. Whether the claim is true depends on what 'automation' means. Doing some tasks and replacing whole jobs give different answers. The surrounding text points to the job-replacement reading, but he did not settle it. Under that reading, the test would be whether generative AI was replacing whole occupations or large parts of the workforce as of mid-2024. That reading also overlaps with his separate view about what generative AI is capable of. The labor evidence is context only. In October 2025, The Register reported a Yale Budget Lab finding of no discernible economy-wide labor disruption in the 33 months after ChatGPT's release (e1). The same report cited a Stanford Digital Economy Lab study. That study found a 13 percent relative employment decline for recent college graduates in the occupations most exposed to AI (e2). Neither finding answers the definitional question, so the claim is not scored.
limitations: Both context items come from one news report summarizing the studies, not from the studies themselves.
The Yale finding covers the 33 months after ChatGPT's November 2022 release, and much of that period comes after the July 2024 post. The report does not give the period the Stanford study covers.
Employment studies measure labor-market effects. They cannot settle whether generative AI counts as 'automation'.

statement.excerpt: And as a reminder, generative AI is not automation.

from_speaker: context: OpenAI would need to "replace entire chunks of the labor force"
context: "automating chunks of the economy" is a use case he does not believe generative AI can meet
our_interpretation: The sentence describes what kind of thing generative AI is. It names no measure, period, or threshold.

In context, the fairest reading is that generative AI does not replace whole jobs or large parts of the workforce. It does not deny that it can do some tasks. That reading partly restates his separate, forward-looking view about what generative AI is capable of, so it is half observation and half capability judgment.
Whether a tool counts as 'automation' depends on a definition he did not give. Any verdict would depend on a definition the evaluator picks, so the claim is treated as not adjudicable.
criteria.support_condition: Not scoreable. Under the context reading, evidence that, as of mid-2024, generative AI was not replacing whole occupations or large parts of the labor force would fit the claim.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Not scoreable. Under the context reading, evidence that, by mid-2024, generative AI was replacing whole jobs at economy-relevant scale would cut against it.

evidence.explanation: Under the job-replacement reading, this points his way: researchers found no economy-wide labor disruption from late 2022 to 2025. It does not settle whether generative AI 'is automation' in a definitional sense.
